title: Facing the King's Indian: White's classical race on the queenside

difficulty.label: 1.d4 player whose opponent chose the King's Indian

objective.summary: Your opponent chose the King's Indian and is planning a pawn storm at your king. The classical answer is not to stop it — it is to win the other race: develop calmly, answer ...Nc6 with d5, and have Ne1-d3 and c5 queued before ...f5 lands. This pack drills that order until the storm stops feeling like an emergency.

planClasses.label: Seal with d5, reroute Ne1-d3, break with c5
planClasses.description: The spine's plan: when the centre closes, White's pawn chain points at the queenside, and every move either queues the c5 break or clears the pieces that will use the c-file. Defensive gestures on the kingside are moves the queenside never gets back.

planClasses.label: Race faster with 9.b4
planClasses.description: Position-specific to this tabiya: skip the Ne1 regroup and start the queenside pawns immediately. Sharper and less forgiving — the b4 pawn is a target and the e4 defence thinner — but the storm meets a storm one tempo sooner.

planClasses.label: Neutralize the g7 bishop when the centre opens
planClasses.description: The fianchettoed bishop is the Indian's engine whenever the long diagonal opens. Trading it or keeping the diagonal closed is a standing sub-goal of every White plan here; the reusable doctrine lives in the shape entry.

annotations: The classical development: knight before bishop, keeping f3 available for the pawn only after the knight later re-routes via e1.
Modest on purpose: the bishop's job is to hold c4 and free the king to castle, not to find a diagonal. Your activity arrives by pawn break, not by piece placement.
The King's Indian strike. You have three honest answers — keep the tension (the spine), trade queens into the Exchange ending, or seal immediately with 7.d5 — and panic is not one of them.
Castle and let Black declare first. Keeping the d4/e5 tension one more move means ...exd4 is always answered by Nxd4 with a comfortable game, so Black usually commits with ...Nc6.
The invitation. The knight attacks d4 hoping you push — and you should: d5 hits it with tempo and closes the centre with YOUR pawn chain pointing at the queenside.
Played with tempo on c6 — the one moment d5 gains a move rather than spending one. From here the game is two races, and yours is on the c-file.
Black reroutes for ...f5. This is YOUR decision point: the patient Ne1 regroup or the immediate 9.b4 bayonet. Both are authored; the comparison is the drill.
The knight clears f3's square for the pawn and heads for d3, the square that pushes c5 and watches the b4-f4 squares at once. Slower than b4, sturdier than b4.
The move Ne1 bought: e4 is now held by a pawn, so ...f5 wins nothing in the centre and ...f4 closes the kingside where your wall already stands.
The storm is released — on schedule, into a prepared position. Play on: Nd3, c5, cxd6 and the c-file against ...f4, ...g5-g4. Count every tempo.

The Bayonet Attack: the queenside pawns move before the pieces regroup. You gain a full tempo of race and accept a looser structure — b4 can be hit by ...a5 and ...Nh5 comes with ideas against f4/g3 squares.

checkpoints.label: 8.d5 — the chains are signed; your game is the queenside
8...Ne7 — patient Ne1 or immediate b4: choose your race
You are past the authored line

deviations.note: 6.h3 keeps Be2 and g4 options open and blunts a later ...Bg4 pin before it exists. A real system with its own theory; no row identity is claimed for this exact move order and none is cited.

7.dxe5 dxe5 8.Qxd8 Rxd8 trades queens on Black's terms of material and yours of temperament: the walked line runs 9.Nxe5 Nxe4 and the fireworks resolve level. It defuses the storm entirely at the price of playing for two results against a prepared opponent. The full sequence was machine-walked as legal chess; no engine has graded it.

7.d5 — the Petrosian Variation — seals immediately, before ...Nc6 can ask the question. Its structural cost: d5 arrives without tempo, and Black's knight keeps the choice of ...Nbd7/...Na6 routes rather than being pushed to e7.

8.Be3 holds the tension with a piece and dares ...Ng4: the walked reply hits the bishop immediately, and the resulting Bg5/h6 dance is a genuine theory battle. Same family of positions, more concrete questions per move.
10.Be3 — the Neo-Classical row — develops before f3, betting that ...f5 can be met with piece pressure on the dark squares. The pack's f3 spine is the traditional order; both are catalogued lines.

feedbackClaims.text: At the 1400/1600/1800 rating bands (Lichess blitz+rapid, 2024-01 through 2026-07), the King's Indian position after 2...g6 was reached 5,353,956 times, scoring 48.0% for White — and 3.Nc3, this pack's preamble, is what 77.5% of White players already choose. The line you are drilling is the mainstream of your own practice.

Against a committed pawn storm, prophylaxis is measured in single moves: f3 because Ne1 freed it, Nd3 because it pushes c5 — each defensive-looking move must also be a race move, or it is a tempo donated to the attack.
d5 is best played at the moment it attacks something: answered to ...Nc6 it gains the race a full move compared to sealing pre-emptively, because the knight must spend a tempo retreating.
